intro: This branch introduces the derivative, which measures how fast something is changing at a single moment. It covers what the derivative means and the rules for calculating it quickly.

VI.2.01.what: The difference between average speed over a trip and your exact speed at one instant. The instant speed is what a speedometer shows.

levels.a: Finds the average rate of change over a stretch, like average speed.
levels.b: Shrinks the stretch smaller and smaller to close in on the instant rate.
levels.c: Explains the instant rate as a speedometer-style reading.
levels.d: Estimates an instant rate from a table of measured values.

VI.2.02.what: Finding the line that just touches a curve at one point (the tangent) by looking at lines through two nearby points.

levels.a: Draws lines through two points on a curve (secant lines).
levels.b: Sees the slopes of these lines settle on one value as the points get closer.
levels.c: Identifies that settled line as the tangent line at the point.
levels.d: Zooms into a smooth curve until it looks straight, matching the tangent.

VI.2.03.what: The official definition of a derivative as a limit: the slope between two points as the gap between them shrinks to nothing.

levels.a: Writes the slope formula between x and a nearby point x plus h.
levels.b: Computes the derivative of x squared directly from the definition.
levels.c: Does the same for one over x and the square root of x.
levels.d: Uses a second version of the definition to find the slope at one specific point.

VI.2.04.what: The different ways derivatives are written, and what each piece of notation means.

levels.a: Reads and writes the "f prime" notation for a derivative.
levels.b: Reads and writes the "dy over dx" notation.
levels.c: Writes the derivative at one specific input, a single number.
levels.d: Gives the units of a derivative, such as meters per second.

VI.2.05.what: A function is differentiable where its graph is smooth enough to have a clear slope. Sharp points and vertical spots are where this fails.

levels.a: Spots sharp corners, where there is no single slope.
levels.b: Spots cusps, where the graph comes to a pointed tip.
levels.c: Spots places where the tangent line is vertical.
levels.d: Explains why a function with a slope at a point must be unbroken there.

VI.2.06.what: Sketching the graph of the derivative by reading slopes off the original graph, and working back the other way.

levels.a: Turns steepness on the original graph into height on the new graph.
levels.b: Marks zeros of the derivative where the original graph is flat.
levels.c: Sketches the whole derivative graph from the original.
levels.d: Works backwards, sketching the original graph from the derivative graph.

VI.2.07.what: The power rule, a shortcut for the derivative of x raised to any power: bring the power down and lower it by one.

levels.a: Uses the power rule for whole-number powers like x cubed.
levels.b: Uses it for negative powers, such as one over x squared.
levels.c: Uses it for fractional powers, such as square roots.
levels.d: Rewrites roots and fractions as powers first, then differentiates.

VI.2.08.what: Basic rules: constants have zero rate of change, multipliers carry through, and sums can be done piece by piece.

levels.a: Knows the derivative of a plain constant is zero.
levels.b: Keeps a number multiplier in front while differentiating.
levels.c: Differentiates sums and differences term by term.
levels.d: Differentiates whole polynomials quickly in one line.

VI.2.09.what: The product rule, for finding the derivative of two things multiplied together.

levels.b: Applies it to a product of two functions.
levels.c: Extends it to a product of three functions.
levels.d: Explains why the answer is not simply the two derivatives multiplied.

VI.2.10.what: The quotient rule, for finding the derivative of one thing divided by another.

levels.b: Applies it to a fraction of two functions.
levels.c: Simplifies the often messy result into a neat final answer.
levels.d: Recognizes when rewriting the fraction first is easier than the quotient rule.

VI.2.11.what: The derivatives of the trigonometry functions, like sine and cosine, which describe waves and rotation.

levels.a: Uses the derivatives of sine and cosine.
levels.b: Uses the derivatives of tangent and secant.
levels.c: Uses the derivatives of cosecant and cotangent.
levels.d: Derives the sine and cosine rules from the limit definition.

VI.2.12.what: The derivatives of exponential functions, which describe growth like compound interest, and of logarithms, which undo them.

levels.a: Uses the fact that e to the x is its own derivative.
levels.b: Differentiates other bases, like 2 to the x.
levels.c: Differentiates the natural logarithm, ln x.

VI.2.13.what: The chain rule, for functions nested inside other functions. Multiply the rate of the outer layer by the rate of the inner layer.

levels.a: Identifies the inside and outside functions of a nested expression.
levels.b: Applies the chain rule once to find a derivative.
levels.c: Applies it several times for functions nested more than two deep.
levels.d: Combines the chain rule with the product and quotient rules.

VI.2.14.what: Finding slopes on curves like circles, where y is mixed in with x and cannot easily be separated out.

levels.a: Differentiates both sides of an equation involving x and y.
levels.b: Recognizes where "dy over dx" appears when differentiating y terms.
levels.c: Rearranges to solve for "dy over dx".
levels.d: Finds the slope of the curve at a specific point.

VI.2.15.what: Finding the derivative of a function that undoes another, such as arcsine undoing sine.

levels.a: Uses the general formula linking the slopes of a function and its inverse.
levels.d: Finds the slope of an inverse function using only a table of values.

VI.2.16.what: Taking the derivative again, and again. The second derivative measures how the rate itself is changing, like acceleration.

levels.a: Finds the second derivative by differentiating twice.
levels.b: Spots patterns to write the derivative after any number of steps.
levels.c: Finds second derivatives for curves where x and y are mixed.
levels.d: Reads and writes the notation for higher derivatives.

VI.2.17.what: A trick for messy derivatives: take the logarithm of both sides first, which turns products and powers into simpler sums.

levels.a: Takes the natural log of both sides of an equation.
levels.b: Differentiates the result and solves for the derivative.
levels.c: Handles functions like x to the power x, with the variable in both places.
levels.d: Uses the method to tame long products and quotients.

VI.2.18.what: Hyperbolic functions are cousins of sine and cosine built from exponentials. One of them describes the shape of a hanging chain.

levels.a: Defines hyperbolic sine and cosine using e to the x.
levels.c: Checks their key identity: cosh squared minus sinh squared equals one.
